action: No action needed; for awareness. Wiz notes that IP-based blocking and IOC sharing do very little against rotating residential proxies, and that the activity carried self-labelling strings such as pentest-recon user agents.
date_note: Wiz's post is dated 23 November 2026; the page gives no earlier day for the report itself.
exec: Wiz reports a rise in successful attacks run by AI agent frameworks such as ARTEX, including one campaign it linked to more than a dozen organisations.
plain: Security firm Wiz says attacks run by AI hacking tools such as ARTEX have grown fast in three weeks, with twenty more incidents disclosed by vendors since its earlier post.
summary: Wiz Research says successful attacks by AI agent frameworks such as ARTEX grew sharply in the last three weeks, with an additional twenty related incidents disclosed by vendors since its Black October post. It tied an ARTEX-Harvester campaign, at varying confidence, to activity at more than a dozen organizations. Wiz says ARTEX activity comes from multiple unrelated operators, not one campaign or threat actor.
title: Wiz: successful AI-agent attacks with ARTEX and similar frameworks grew sharply in three weeks

validation.note: Wiz's own research post read in full (primary for its findings). Figures and the ARTEX-Harvester link are Wiz's own; no second publisher read.

evidence.quote: Since publishing the Black October post, an additional twenty related incidents have been disclosed by vendors.

review.note: Compared date, twenty incidents, more than a dozen organizations, multiple unrelated operators, cloud surface against Wiz post

key_findings: Wiz says it tied one ARTEX-Harvester campaign, at varying confidence, to activity at more than a dozen organizations between late October and mid-November.
Wiz describes ARTEX as an open-source agentic offensive framework with hundreds of forks, and says its activity comes from multiple unrelated operators and should not be read as a single campaign.
Wiz says twenty additional related incidents were disclosed in the three weeks after its Black October post, and that its incident response team saw a 3x increase in engagement requests.
Wiz lists the ways in as stolen or leaked credentials, exposed or vulnerable services, tenant-isolation escapes, upstream breaches and opportunistic spraying often routed through residential proxies.
Wiz says the tooling runs at machine speed and labels its own work, for example with pentest-recon user agents, and that exposed operator consoles leaked prompts and agent transcripts.
recommendations: Rotate exposed credentials and restrict services that still use default credentials.
Do not expose agent control panels to the internet.
Monitor cloud activity for mass secret retrieval, known offensive tool API calls and long-dormant access keys being used.
Focus on behavioural patterns such as speed and breadth rather than IP blocking, which Wiz says does little against rotating residential proxies.

hunt.name: Agentic attacks in the wild IOCs
